MR. CHURCHILL-CONDUCT OF CHAIRMAN OF DEFENCE COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am rising on a question of privilege which affects the rights and privileges of every member of the House of Commons, and particularly affects the conduct of standing and special committees of the house. The normal procedure with regard to these committees, according to my understanding, is that they are masters of their own arrangements concerning the number of meetings and the times at which these meetings may be held. Normally these arrangements are arrived at by unanimous consent or by consultation in the steering committee and, infrequently, by a motion which is debated and settled by the committee as a whole. The latter method is rarely used.
The chairman of a standing or special committee, according to my understanding, has no rights or authority greater than those enjoyed by the chairman of the committee of the whole house, and certainly not equal to those of Mr. Speaker. My understanding has always been that committees are conducted according to the rules of the House of Commons as they are applicable; that the rules of debate apply in committees as they do in the house, as do similarly the rules pertaining to motions and amendments.
[DOT] (11:10 a.m.)
I am drawing your attention, sir-and I think we will have to get this settled-to what I term absolutely autocratic action on the part of the chairman of the defence committee this morning at eleven o'clock. At eleven o'clock this morning the chairman made this statement which I copied down, and which I reaffirm because he repeated it. His statement was "We will meet this afternoon at 3.30".
We received notice of a meeting of the committee for 9.30 this morning which we observed, and that meeting was held. We received no notice of a meeting at 3.30 this afternoon. In the committee at eleven o'clock
no motion that we should meet this afternoon at 3.30 was put forward or received.

Yes, it is even worse. I will change that statement to read two o'clock instead of 3.30, which is an even more arbitrary decision than I imagined it to be. As I say, no motion came before the committee and there was no opportunity for discussion.
I simply raised this point with the chairman and I jotted down his words and asked whether he was arbitrarily making that ruling.
If this is permitted to become an established practice, Mr. Speaker, every committee chairman will set himself up with greater authority than you yourself enjoy-because you operate within the rules-and will determine on his own authority and at his own wish when, and I suppose where, meetings may be held. There is nothing to prevent the autocratic chairman of the defence committee from calling a meeting for tomorrow, or for Sunday, or for tonight, or for 3 a.m. tomorrow morning. This is how far the matter has gone. Unless some restraint can be placed upon this committee chairman-and I hope this restraint will then be observed and followed by other committee chairmen-we as members of this house will have our rights and privileges taken away from us. It is a shocking state of affairs, sir, that a standing committee of the House of Commons should be conducted in this arbitrary fashion, as a result of which hon. members are prevented from carrying out their duties effectively.
There is no excuse for this type of arbitrary action, sir, because this committee has been meeting every day of each week now for four weeks, sometimes twice a day and sometimes three times a day, for a total of 39 meetings. It is doing effective work of the greatest national importance. Yet here are its members being subjected to arbitrary action, sir, action which you yourself would never countenance and have never attempted to take in the House of Commons, because you operate within the rules.

Speaking to this point of order, Mr. Speaker, I wish to clarify the picture for the hon. member for Skeena. I am surprised that he should make so free with something he knows nothing about. The incident in question occurred at eleven o'clock when the chairman made his ruling, gave his order and adjourned the meeting. There was no opportunity at all to speak to the matter, and because he adjourned the meeting summarily we had no chance to complain about the action of the Chair.
[DOT] (11:20 a.m.)
I should like to say further that it had been understood in the committee-I am not sure I can go as far as to say it had been agreed -that we would not meet Friday afternoon. I think this is borne out by the notice of meetings, on which only one meeting at 9.30 this morning appeared. These notices generally cover the meetings for the day. So I think I am supported in my contention that the understanding was that we would not meet on Friday afternoon.
The position is, then, that the chairman hianself made a declaration as to what the committee would do and when it would meet, though the custom is that as a rule these matters are decided by agreement; if there is no agreement a motion is made and a vote is taken. We try to avoid votes; in my mind there is not much doubt that general agreement usually is reached.
This question of privilege is by way of an appeal from the ruling of the chairman of a committee. The new rules provide for appeals to the Speaker from rulings made by the chairman of the committee of the whole house. I do not think there has yet been an occasion under our new rules when anyone has asked Your Honour to hear an appeal against a ruling made by the chairman of a
Conduct of Chairman of Defence Committee committee. I am not sure that our new provisional rules are clear enough in this respect to give the Chair any clear guidance; I do not believe there is any precedent either for or against my suggestion that Your Honour has authority to hear an appeal of this kind, though it is a fact that in general the rules governing the committee of the whole house apply to the proceedings of committees of the house. It is true that each committee has the right to conduct its own business, but this is subject to the general rules governing committees; and except where special provision is made the same general rules govern committees as govern the committee of the whole.
Therefore, since a ruling by the chairman of the committee of the whole house is subject to appeal to the Speaker, I submit that the same applies to a ruling made by the chairman of a committee and that we have the right to ask Your Honour to hear such an appeal. In doing so I ask Your Honour to bear in mind that this decision was taken arbitrarily, and that there was no opportunity to discuss it. The chairman adjourned the meeting immediately so that no dissenting voice should be heard.
In these circumstances I believe Your Honour should go out of your way, if necessary, to so interpret our rules that justice will be done and that the proceedings of our committees will not only be properly conducted but that the appearance that we can act as honourable gentlemen in the proper conduct of our affairs may be maintained. I submit this can best be done by Your Honour making the ruling which I have suggested.

I should think the only people who would be in a position to comment on the developments in the committee are those who witnessed what happened there this morning. What happened in the committee I believe is something that neither the Secretary of State for External Affairs nor the Prime Minister would condone.
I might comment on what the chairman of the committee himself said as to his duties as chairman. He referred to the difficulty experienced by chairmen in other committees. He mentioned the fact that some members who chair committees of this house, because they are attending their first parliament and have inadequate knowledge of the rules and procedures as well as inadequate experience, are running into considerable difficulty. In reflecting upon these other chairmen it would be fair to say that possibly he had in mind the chairman of the fisheries committee.
What happened this morning at what we might call the eleventh hour was that a member tried to put a motion to the chair in respect of meeting this afternoon. In all fairness to the chairman-and he can contradict this statement or accept it, but this is the understanding I have-I think he had some doubt in his mind as to whether there
Conduct of Chairman of Defence Committee was a motion before the committee to meet this afternoon. While members on both sides of the committee were speaking-and there is no doubt that sides have been established in the committee, one against the other-and while he was trying to make up his mind as to whether there was a motion before the committee, the house bells were ringing. At that point the chairman raised his gavel and indicated to the committee that there would be a further meeting this afternoon at two o'clock and thereby cut off any further discussion in respect of any of the rules of the house which are applicable to committees.
When the hon. member for Essex West and the hon. member for Skeena indicate that under the rules the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre had an opportunity to discuss this matter, this is not the case. There was absolutely no opportunity to discuss the rules or anything else. The fact that the chairman raised his gavel, adjourned the meeting, said that we would meet at two o'clock, and then rose from his position as chairman without further ado should be a clear indication that there was no opportunity in committee to discuss the matter of the meeting this afternoon. subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF CHANGES IN MANPOWER MOBILITY PROGRAM

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Marchand (Minister of Manpower and Immigration):
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF CHANGES IN MANPOWER MOBILITY PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to inform the house of changes the
March 3. 19G7

government proposes to make, to become effective on April 1, to strengthen the manpower mobility program.
It will be recalled that this program was introduced late in 1965. A worker who has been unemployed for four months may qualify for a grant to help him to move with his family to another area where there is a job for him. A worker who has been unemployed for less than four months may obtain a loan for the same purpose.
Parliament in this fiscal year provided $3,500,000 for grants, and a revolving fund of $5 million was established for the loans. In the first 12 months, however, there were 1,207 grants and 982 loans amounting to a total combined value of approximately $1,185,000.
Clearly the program is not providing as much help as was intended. The reason is that we recognized from the beginning that it would be a difficult program to administer, and that therefore we should start cautiously, broadening the program as we gain experience. I took one step in that direction last April by providing that people living in an area where a shut-down or a lay-off removed a major source of employment would be eligible for grants and not be subject to the previous requirement that they be unemployed for four months.
We are now ready to take a further major step. The following three changes are proposed. First, we will drop altogether the restrictive condition about four months' unemployment. That is to say, this will no longer be partially a loan program. Any man who is unemployed, or has been notified of his permanent lay-off, will be entitled to a grant if there is little prospect of suitable employment in his home community and there is a definite job for him to go to in another area.
Second, we propose to amend the grants to lessen what is often the main obstacle to moving, in that the man who owns his own home faces considerable expense and even loss in selling a house in an area where there is unemployment and has to obtain what is likely to be more expensive housing in another area. To offset this we will make a grant of $500 when the former home is sold or when a new one is purchased.
Third, we propose to make small grants to enable unemployed people to look for work in the nearest area where there are better opportunities than in their home district. This grant will cover the person's return travel expenses and, if he has dependants, a modest allowance to help support them while he is
Changes in Manpower Mobility Program away. This allowance will be up to $20 a week for the first dependant, $30 a week for two dependants, and $40 a week for three or more. The allowance will be available for a maximum of four weeks.

Mr. Speaker, I believe that these changes greatly improve our mobility program. They do not, however, make it complete. The people who most need help in relocation are not always unemployed but are people such as marginal farmers with very low incomes from their present occupations. We want to help these underemployed people but it will be appreciated that there are difficult problems of definition and administration. We therefore want our officers to gain experience with the broader grants for unemployed before making the further extension of coverage.
Accordingly, the government plans that, while the changes I have announced will take effect on April 1, further changes to cover underemployed people will be introduced with effect on September 1.
I would like to emphasize, Mr. Speaker, that we will implement this broadened program in a way that co-ordinates it with the industrial development activities of the provinces and of other governmental agencies. Generally speaking, we will be helping workers to move to the nearest community where there are jobs. It is not our intention to divert manpower from emerging employment in nearby areas or elsewhere in a province, but rather to make it possible for people to move to such employment and thus strengthen regional and provincial development programs.
There is one final point. This program now operates on the basis of regulations. That is appropriate to the developmental stage that it has been in and that will continue for some time yet. By the fall, however, I think we will have brought it to a form that can be regarded as fairly complete. The government's intention therefore is at that time to introduce legislation by which parliament would give the program a permanent basis.

I think the minister should look at this aspect to ascertain whether some other plan could be put into effect which would be more helpful to people who have to move to areas where houses might be available but where this flat $500 grant would not be sufficient.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF CHANGES IN MANPOWER MOBILITY PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we greet with approval the improvements in the manpower mobility program which the minister announced today. Having said that, however, I think it is necessary to point out to the minister and the government that over the past couple of years organizations such as the Canadian Labour Congress and its affiliated unions have been extremely critical of the inadequacies of the existing program as well as the projected programs. The announcements the minister makes today are welcome, but if we compare them with the need illustrated recently for facilities for the retraining of auto workers, the inadequacies are pointed up.
According to the minister, 5,700 auto workers are being laid off as a result of the auto pact, yet we do not have facilities for training more than a small percentage of these displaced workers. It is obvious, therefore, we have a long way to go before we could consider the manpower program of the government adequate. I join with the hon. member for Ontario in expressing concern over the $500 grant announced by the minister because it will prove inadequate, as have most of the steps the government has taken to date. This grant will be of small help to a worker who may be laid off in Oshawa or in Cape Breton, where the coal industry is in trouble, if he has to move to a city like Toronto in which the cost of housing is high. The $500 will be of little help in the purchase or rental of another house.
So, Mr. Speaker, while joining with the spokesman for the official opposition in welcoming these small changes, I suggest to the minister that he still has a long way to go before his department has established a policy which will meet the needs of Canadian workers who are being displaced at a rapid rate in this technological age.

the transfers that are going on all over Canada a substantial administrative problem could arise. While we wish the minister success in these amendments to the mobility program, there must be far more than has been indicated so far or I am sure the minister is going to be severely upset.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on several occasions recently hon. members have inquired about the discussions I have held with farm machinery companies concerning recently announced price increases.
During recent weeks I have met with representatives of the major manufacturers of farm machinery. At these meetings we discussed the question of price increases for farm machinery during 1967, and in particular increases while the work of the royal commission on farm machinery is under way, the lines of equipment which would be most affected and the reasons for any proposed increases. In these discussions I indicated my desire to keep any price increases to a minimum, particularly while the royal commission on farm machinery prices was deliberating.
Report of Discussions on Farm Machinery
I have been very much encouraged by the response from the farm machinery companies. Generally speaking I have obtained assurances that price increases to be effected in 1967 will not result in overall increases of more than 2 per cent to 3 per cent. On some individual items price increases may be somewhat higher, but for other items no price increases whatever are expected.
Part of the price increase in many cases is the result of product improvement. The effect of this on prices was estimated by various companies to be about a third to one half of the price increase. In certain cases the price increases are due to factors beyond the control of companies operating in Canada. Some companies import considerable quantities of their components from the United States and the United Kingdom. Price increases on components from these sources have been 3 per cent to 4 per cent. One company, for example, imports 90 per cent of its Canadian sales. The house will appreciate that in a case like this, price increases outside our borders have a direct bearing on the prices which such companies have to charge in Canada.
The companies in turn have pointed out to me the increased costs which they face in 1967 and which they are not in a position to absorb out of their earnings without affecting their ability to obtain new capital. Increased costs mentioned by the machinery companies were 3.5 per cent to 4.5 per cent on materials, 7 per cent on wages, higher borrowing rates and increased transportation charges of 10 per cent on materials. Mr. Speaker, the farmers of this country will be delighted to learn that the government has finally ascertained that there has been an increase in the prices of farm machinery, something the farmers have been aware of for the last four years. to be very disappointed in the announcement that has been made this morning, because following previous announcements of the Minister of Agriculture when he first took office they anticipated that should there be a drastic increase in the prices of farm machinery something would be done about it. On the other hand, the minister has indicated that there could be an even greater increase in the prices of certain specified machines.
Anyone who buys farm machinery, Mr. Speaker, knows that under normal circumstances most of it is purchased during the first three months of the year. This announcement has been delayed until the major portion of the machinery required for the 1967 season is either now in the hands of the farmers or has been contracted for.
I would take issue with the minister's figure of 2 per cent to 3 per cent. Figures just released by the Dominion Bureau of Statistics would seem to indicate that in the 1965 season there was an 10 per cent over-all increase in farm machinery prices. As far as the 1966 season is concerned, it has been pointed out in this house to the minister that in some instances prices went up 8 per cent. With the increase now indicated by the minister of some 2 per cent to 3 per cent for this year, this means that in 1967 the farmers of this nation could be faced with increases in prices on some lines of machinery of 20 per cent over the 1965 prices.
Such an increase is not justified, Mr. Speaker, and I suggest that the farmers of this nation have every reason to blame this government for not bringing in a policy which would hold down farm machinery prices. That was what the farmers expected,

First he said he was encouraged by the discussions he had had with farm machinery manufacturers; then he tried to justify price increases. I understand that the cost of parts coming in from the United States and the United Kingdom have increased by 3 per cent or 4 per cent; yet the Dominion Bureau of Statistics report says that substantially over 10 per cent more was being charged for these

implements in 1966 than was being charged in 1965.
Would the royal commission looking into this matter make an interim report on this situation? We have no satisfactory explanation why price increases are justified. Those increases ought to be explained. It is all very well to say that costs have increased so much more for labour and so much more for other things, but are those increases justified? The royal commission was set up to investigate this very situation.
In conclusion may I say that farmers are not satisfied with things as they are. We hope there will be some governmental investigation and a report with respect to whether farm machinery companies have been asking for unjustified increases.

AMENDMENTS RESPECTING TAKING OF ADMISSIONS OR CONFESSIONS
speechtext: for leave to introduce Bill No. C-276, to amend the Canada Evidence Act (incriminating statements).

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING TAKING OF ADMISSIONS OR CONFESSIONS
speechtext: Explain.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING TAKING OF ADMISSIONS OR CONFESSIONS
speechtext:
The purpose of this bill is to amend the Canada Evidence Act to put into that act some of the principles enunciated by the United States Supreme Court in 1966, according to which any admission or confession made while the accused is in custody cannot be used by the prosecution unless it proves that the police warned the suspect that he may remain silent and that anything he says may be held against him; also, that he has the right to have a lawyer present during interrogation.
If the suspect desires a lawyer but cannot afford one he cannot be questioned unless the crown appoints a lawyer and that lawyer is present. If the suspect confesses after receiving the required warning, but without having the benefit of counsel, the burden is on the prosecution to prove a knowing waiver by the accused-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING TAKING OF ADMISSIONS OR CONFESSIONS
speechtext:
Order, please. I think the hon. member knows that according to the rules his statement should be brief. I suggest that perhaps brevity is being forgotten this morning.
March 3. 1967

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING TAKING OF ADMISSIONS OR CONFESSIONS
speechtext:
May I conclude with one more sentence. The burden is on the prosecution to prove a knowing waiver by the accused, and the interrogation will be conducted in such a way, and will be taken to show a lack of waiver unless proof to the contrary is provided.

Equalization Payments to Provinces Mr. Monleilh: Mr. Chairman, last evening the Minister of Finance and the Secretary of State outlined in broad terms the contents of this resolution and the intent of the bill which will be before us at the conclusion of the debate on the resolution. I think this intent represents probably as important a step in federal-provincial relations as has been taken in this house for many years. As has been announced, this resolution and the bill to follow are the outcome of discussions with the provinces at a meeting last October between the Minister of Finance and his counterparts in the provincial governments. At that time major changes were proposed to the provinces and the Minister of Finance outlined them in the following words:
[DOT] (2:10 p.m.)
Major changes were proposed in the following fields: the occupancy of tax fields or tax sharing; provincial revenue equalization arrangements; provincial revenue stabilization arrangements; federal financial assistance in respect of post-secondary education: a new form of federal compensation to the provinces in respect of well established shared cost programs in the health and welfare field; and finally, a new federal program for the occupational training of adults in lieu of the technical and vocational training argreements which expire on March 31 this year.
The Minister of Finance suggested that there were certain principles which he had presented to the tax structure committee whose findings were subsequently presented to the federal-provincial meetings of finance ministers. Some six principles were evolved to guide the committee in its deliberations.
The minister also mentioned that the federal government maintained the following: -that so long as provincial governments had access to sufficient tax fields and so long as provincial revenues were equalized fairly, the provinces should impose their own taxes to finance their own programs.
Certainly this is a most important statement with which I cannot disagree, but I would like to withhold judgment until I see the bill. The minister indicated last night that when the bill is before us he will give us information as to just what the net gain or loss will be to the provinces under the new arrangements. He also stated:
Instead of selecting certain taxes at given or standard rates and equalizing their yield to the level of the top two provinces, the proposed formula will take into account all provincial revenues, at average provincial rates, and will bring the revenue yield in all provinces up to the national average yield.
[The Chairman.]

Just what this will mean in dollars and cents remains to be seen. I cannot help but agree that it is a very important principle.
The Minister of Finance last evening and the Secretary of State today have put on record certain tables. Sufficient time has not been available to permit me to analyse these figures but they will be helpful when we study the bill in detail.
The Minister of Finance made a statement to the effect that the federal government now proposes to extend the stabilization provision to all provincial revenues and proposes to remove the five-year limit which has applied to the stabilization provision as well as to the equalization provisions. Stabilization is to be provided on a continuing basis as a protection to the provinces against sharp declines in revenue. I am wondering whether these agreements are to be in effect forever or to what degree they are subject to discontinuance by either party concerned. If they are to be extended beyond the five-year limit I wonder what the duration of that extension will be.
Until a change of government.

I can assure the hon. member for Essex East that he will not be around when this matter is discussed next because I doubt very much that he will be re-elected in that auto city of his. I am sure I need not impress on the house either the crucial importance of this matter to the future of our country or the very difficult and complex problems posed in trying to deal with it.

The matter which must concern the house, Mr. Chairman, is what the long term effect of this legislation will be, not only with respect to the ability of the federal government to discharge its responsibilities but also the effect it will have on the ability of the provinces and municipalities to discharge their responsibilities. In his statement last night, as recorded at page 13681 of Hansard, the minister set forth six basic principles with which I am sure no one could disagree. However, the minister did not demonstrate the extent to which the measures he is proposing will give effect to the principles he enunciated.
By way of illustration, I will refer to the first principle. The minister stated that the fiscal arrangements should give both the federal and provincial governments access to fiscal resources sufficient to discharge their responsibilities under the constitution. I must
Equalization Payments to Provinces say that from the minister's statement last night I am far from convinced that the provinces and municipalities can discharge their responsibilities within the terms of the tax sharing arrangement which the minister announced.
I understand that the tax structure committee prepared some figures which indicated that by 1972, on the basis of a 7 per cent annual rate of growth in the gross national product, the federal government will have a surplus of $727 million but the provinces and municipalities will have deficits of $2.1 billion. It is suggested also, predicated on a 6 per cent annual rate of growth in the gross national product, that by 1972 the federal government will still have a small surplus but that the provinces and municipalities will have deficits of $2.4 billion. If these compilations have not been produced by the tax structure committee I hope the minister will give us what their estimate was when he presents the legislation or before we close the debate on this resolution. If these figures are correct, what they really mean is that the provinces and municipalities are now going to operate within a very restricted fiscal framework.
The provinces will have three alternatives. One will be to cut services. The second will be to raise other taxes which are outside of the agreement. The third will be to do a great deal of deficit financing by borrowing. I think any one of these proposals would be disastrous for Canada. It seems to me, Mr. Chairman, that while as members of parliament we are primarily concerned with the financial problems of the government of Canada we cannot for one moment be indifferent to the welfare of the provinces and municipalities. After all, if the provinces and municipalities are unable to discharge their constitutional responsibilities with respect to education, health, welfare, roads and industrial development, then no matter what the federal government does Canada will not prosper and grow at the rate which might otherwise be the case. Therefore, in examining this legislation when it comes before us we must be concerned with the overall effect on all three levels of government of these tax sharing proposals.
I am concerned, for instance, about the decision to include all provincial revenues in the determination of the equalization payments. I think this can work to the great disadvantage of some areas of Canada and can produce great inequalities in the equalization formula. I am concerned that it is being predicated upon the average income

Equalization Payments to Provinces for Canada rather than bringing the provinces up to the level of the highest province or at least to the average of the two highest provinces. It would seem to me we are making a retrograde step by saying to the provinces, we will only bring you up to the national average. If we are going to have equality of opportunity for people in all parts of Canada, if we are going to remove any disparity between Canadians in different areas, surely we ought to average the equalization payments to the highest province in Canada and not to the national average.
We will want to examine these proposals more closely when the legislation comes before us. I think the reference to assistance to post-secondary education is a very necessary step and a very welcome innovation. I am sure the provinces must be concerned, as we must be concerned, about the fact that what the Lord giveth the Lord taketh away. While the government is proposing to give greater assistance to post-secondary education, it is proposing to discontinue its grants with respect to technical and vocational education. We will want to go into that in detail to see what the net effect is for the provinces.
It is a long phase-out.

The minister says it is a long phase-out. This is true, and that is what worries me about it. The provinces might be induced to accept a program which may be slightly more beneficial this year and next year, but we have to take the long view. If the figures I quoted earlier are correct and by 1972 the provinces and municipalities will be deeper in debt as a result of these proposals, then of course a long phase-out will not meet their problems.
The other thing that concerns me is that the provinces are being asked to accept responsibility for some of the shared cost programs in return for tax abatements. These shared cost programs have escalated in the past and, in my opinion, over the next 10 or 15 years will escalate in almost goemetric progression. Any province getting into difficulty with programs like hospital insurance, medicare or the old age assistance program will have no alternative but to cut back these programs. The federal government may feel comfortable in that it has washed its hands of responsibility by giving the provinces certain tax abatements. But if, Mr. Chairman, they cut these programs back we will have lost the measure of national social security which we provided when we instituted programs like

Therefore, Mr. Chairman, there are a great many questions that have to be answered before we can give our support to these tax sharing proposals. I am hopeful that when the ministers make their speeches on second reading of the bill we will have a greater amount of detail to enable us to make a better comparison of the projected revenues which the provinces can anticipate under the legislation compared with what they could expect to receive under the existing tax sharing arrangements. I think some of the suggestions made by the ministers will undoubtedly make for improvement, but I am very fearful that we are manoeuvring the provinces into an inflexible taxation framework which will have the result of restricting their ability to keep pace with the growth of the Canadian economy and to meet the increasing demands of their people and of the times in which we live. Therefore, Mr. Chairman, we will look forward to the statements which will be made by the ministers when the bill is brought forward, and at that time we will be able to deal more exhaustively with the proposals which are being placed before us.

Mr. Chairman, the resolution before us, as has been stated, deals with renewing and in some cases changing the tax sharing arrangements between the provinces and the federal government. A very cursory examination of the remarks made by the two ministers last night as well as of the resolution indicates that probably this is all that can be done at this time owing to the fact that no agreement was reached between the two levels of government at the conference held on this subject last fall as to the future arrangements.
In looking over some of the proposals that the federal government has offered the provinces-and this aspect took up a very large portion of the minister's statement last night-it seems to me that there are some serious inequities which are now coming home to roost. Unfortunately we are now going to be asked to perpetuate some of them. For example, I should like the minister to explain why it is that in the table on page 13687 of Hansard showing the yield at national average province revenue rate for the other 12 revenue sources there is included an item of $93,083,000 in general sales tax for the province of Alberta. The province of Alberta does not have any such tax.
March 3, 1967	COMMONS
I have known for some time that the federal government has assumed that the province of Alberta does have access to revenue from a sales tax. It seems to me that there is something fundamentally wrong with so-called federal-provincial relations when the federal government assumes that a province has a revenue in respect of which in actual fact there is no provincial legislation. That is not to say, of course, that if it so wished the province of Alberta could not impose such a sales tax. It so happens that under the constitution of Canada the provincial legislatures have the right to say whether or not they are going to impose this, that or any other tax. Yet in this table it is claimed that the province of Alberta has a revenue source of $93 million by way of sales tax.
I think we have reached a pretty serious situation so far as federal-provincial relations are concerned, when the federal government now uses federal money as the basis for requiring or prodding provincial governments to levy certain taxes. I had hoped that this was not going to be the attitude of the federal government, but obviously it is. Therefore we will have to do what we can to keep the federal government within its own area of jurisdiction and see that it treats all provinces essentially the same.
As the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam has pointed out, we have no disagreement with the principles underlying the federal proposals for new tax sharing arrangements; there is no question of that. I am not going to refer to them because they are well known to the members of this house as well as to the provincial governments. However, there are some other matters which have been introduced recently into the tax sharing arrangements which form the basis of the program and which in my view are completely unacceptable.
We know that when the equalization payments were formulated a number of years ago there were only three tax bases-personal income tax, corporate income tax and succession duties. This was changed by the former Conservative government in 1961 and resource revenue was included as a fourth basis. There has never been any satisfactory explanation for this inclusion except the penalizing of the government of Alberta. That the federal government certainly did, because the province of Alberta was penalized by approximately $30 million to $40 million a year as a result of the inclusion of this particular form of revenue in the calculation of the equalization payments.

It has always seemed strange to me, Mr. Chairman, looking back to that period, that there rwere 17 Conservative members out of a possible 17 from the province of Alberta at that time and not one of them stood up in the house and defended the people they represented notwithstanding the fact that the change was going to cost them millions of dollars every year. I do not think we can lay all of the blame on the present government when it was the previous government which introduced that change. However, the present government certainly should have seen the inequity in this kind of arrangement and remedied it.
This government did not introduce any other additions to the tax base. They did not include, for example, the retail sales tax which many of the provinces had in effect at the time. That source of revenue was not used to calculate the equalization payments. Even the province of Saskatchewan is now reaching the point where the inclusion of resource revenue is starting to hurt them. In fact, a few weeks ago the premier of Saskatchewan said that the new arrangement is a cruel blow to his province. He had expected something like $35 million, I believe, in 1967 in equalization payments, but according to the table that has been put before us Saskatchewan now moves out of the "have not" class into the "have" class and does not get one cent. Conservative members might well go back to 1961 to find out what originated the arbitrary inclusion of resource revenues in the tax base. It is there, Mr. Chairman, and it is unjust. It is even more unjust now because the federal government is assuming that Alberta has a sales tax when it has not.
[DOT] (2:40 p.m.)
I submit that there are many injustices in this whole arrangement. I am hoping that we will have further federal-provincial agreements concluded or federal-provincial conferences held very soon to straighten out some of these injustices and to treat all provinces in Canada and all citizens of those provinces equally. It is about time we realized that some of the revenue produced in Alberta and British Columbia has been from the sale of capital assets. These sales will not be repeated year by year to bring additional revenue. Yet these sales of assets are treated as things which ordinarily produce revenue. Not all provinces do that sort of thing.

I now wish to turn to the statement made by the Secretary of State with respect to future federal contributions to be made to post-secondary education. I will not go into details but I have discussed this matter with people interested in the subject.
A number of things bother me, the most important one being the matter of definitions. What kinds of costs or expenses will these grants be paid for? The minister last night said something about costs being paid with respect to students who have achieved junior matriculation level. The government will be prepared to pay $15 per capita for education beyond that level. The whole question is fuzzy. What is junior matriculation? At the moment in Alberta junior matriculation is reached at the end of grade 11. Is that what the minister has in mind? If I understand correctly, junior matriculation is the point at which young people may leave high school. Could the minister expand on this point?
It seems to me that post-secondary education ought to be defined in a more satisfactory way than by saying it is education after certain scholastic standards are reached. The program should apply to vocational and training institutions as well as to universities. The government could pay up to 50 per cent of the operating and capital costs of these institutions. That would be easier than trying to pay the money to individuals or on their behalf after they have attained a certain scholastic standing.
I am greatly concerned about high school drop-outs. Those who do not have junior matriculation often need to go to vocational training institutions, of which there are many in this country. High school drop-outs have as much right to grants and financial assistance from the federal treasury as those attaining junior matriculation level.
If I interpret what the minister has said there will be no provision in the bill for students to attend vocational and technical training schools unless they have their junior matriculation. In many provinces junior matriculation level is not attained until students are in grade 12. In one or two provinces they do not attain that level until grade 13.
One of the major problems is that those who drop out of high school, often without junior matriculation, will not be able to

attend a technical or vocational training school and those young people are the very ones who will be found on the unemployment rolls.
Item No. 134 on the order paper is a resolution providing for the training of adults wishing to undertake occupational training. But conditions are attached. They must have entered the labour force and they must have been unemployed for a long period before they can qualify for assistance under this proposal.
The Secretary of State and the Minister of Finance would be well advised to try to reach agreement with the provinces to pay 50 per cent of the costs, or whatever the figure may be, for vocational training schools rather than going through the complexities of ascertaining the scholastic standing of students and making the payments on the basis of their standing. I presume this argument has been advanced previously to the Secretary of State. If it has been rejected I should like to know why. Why are we becoming involved with students rather than with schools?
The problem must be met in one of two ways. The provinces will have to assume the full financial responsibility for training young people who do not reach junior matriculation standards or, alternatively, the young people will have to leave school, enter the labour market, be unemployed for a long period and then receive help from the federal government. The latter course is not desirable.
The vocational and technical training program is useful. Among other things it has provided much of the capital for building such schools. I can perhaps exonerate myself in the eyes of the Conservative party by paying a tribute and saying that this was their program. It has been appreciated and has done at least all it was intended to do and perhaps more. But now it will be phased out. Technical and vocational training schools, at least in Alberta, train young people who have dropped out of high school. They give them the kind of training to fit them to find their place in the labour market.
Taking the two resolutions together, it appears that there is a serious gap in federal contributions to a particular group of people needing financial assistance. I hope the minister will explain why this way of doing things has been chosen. Why has the government not chosen to pay 50 per cent of the cost of operating technical and vocational training

Worse than that, Mr. Chairman, they not only fail to give federal leadership but they are starting to withdraw from a field in which the federal government had participated.
The hon. member for Queens referred to the minister of labour in the previous administration, the hon. member for Ontario, and the bold program he started in 1960 which the provinces all joined. I wonder if the members of this committee truly appreciate the extent of that program and the fact that all provinces participated fully. One of
Equalization Payments to Provinces the members to the left mentioned that federal participation involved a sum of over $600 million. Well, Mr. Chairman, during a three year period about 330,000 places were provided for students in vocational and technical training schools.
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
The area I come from is not one of the great industrial areas of the country, but several vocational schools were built there under this program two or three years ago and they are filled to capacity. In spite of this expansion during the last two years, unfortunately applicants for vocational training are still being turned down in large numbers. That indicates the state of the program at the present time, Mr. Chairman. Nevertheless, where would we in Canada be today if the federal government under the party to which I belong had not taken some initiative and trodden very carefully, so as to recognize not only the problems under the constitution but to institute a program which provided over 330,000 student places in two and a half to three years. Over 800 new schools or additions to existing schools were built during that two and a half to three year period and over $1,200 million was spent by the federal and provincial governments combined on that building program.
I suggest there is even greater need for education and skilled manpower in this day and age. In spite of the manpower problems which have arisen during the last two or three months as a result of the auto pact and in other areas as well, we would have been in an even more precarious position today had not the former government taken some initiative. The vocational training program alone shows that when a federal government is prepared to move in and take the lead and also respect the provincial jurisdiction, the provinces will also move into the vacuum. In 1960 there was a vacuum, but fortunately for Canada the government of that day stepped in to fill it.
We are now withdrawing and throwing the problem back to the provinces. Some provinces are capable of doing a good job whereas others are faced with certain problems. But the point is that the federal government is not providing national leadership. I can well understand the concern of the public over the fundamental distinction which is being made between guide lines for medicare but not for education. I should like to hear the Minister of Finance or the minister for health or somebody else on that side try to rationalize
13734	COMMONS
Equalization Payments to Provinces the apparent contradiction that exists in this proposition, which involves provincial jurisdiction.
There is another problem in connection with the transfer to the provinces of certain percentages of corporation and personal income taxes. In effect they are unconditional grants made to the provinces for their educational programs. Just as an aside, Mr. Chairman, and following upon what the hon. member for Queens said, I might point out that there was a good flow of information passing between federal and provincial representatives during the conference last fall. The initial proposals made by the federal government were somewhat confusing and the visiting provincial representatives were somewhat caught by surprise when they read about some of them in the newspapers even before they got to the conference table. But I think the minister and his officials are to be given credit for their give and take attitude with regard to some of the initial proposals, and the final results of the conference will undoubtedly be enshrined within the subject matter of the bill which is to follow this resolution.
I appreciate, Mr. Chairman, that there are two points of view in connection with transferring a percentage of corporation and personal income taxes to the provinces. Some provinces and certainly some of the university officials are most concerned that these unconditional grants which are made to the provinces may not find their way into the university coffers. There have been examples in the not too distant past of moneys given to the provinces for educational purposes which did not find their way into the university stream.
Again, Mr. Chairman, this is an area, quite separate and apart from technical and vocational training, from which the federal government has withdrawn. It is an area which I think involves one of the most fluid segments of our society. The hon. member for Burna-by-Richmond quoted a speech made by the Secretary of State some time ago in which she said that education has no boundaries. In this day and age there is a much greater flow of manpower and skilled tradesmen from one province to another, but I would suggest there is not quite such a great flow in the vocational area as there is in the academic field. University graduates in my part of the country have to travel to other provinces because they cannot become absorbed in the rather limited economic climate prevailing in the Atlantic area.

DEBATES	March 3, 1967
This means, Mr. Chairman, that in certain parts of Canada there is a tremendous influx of one of the most fluid segments of society. In other areas the federal government is withdrawing from this mainstream of society, leaving its control strictly to the provinces, and is hiding behind the strait-jacket of the constitution.
Three or four months ago the minister of health was bold enough to stand up time and again to defend the medicare program, a program which touches the very areas from which the Minister of Finance is now trying to withdraw. No wonder the public are looking for some leadership and direction in this area, Mr. Chairman, and it seems to me they are somewhat bewildered at this apparent paradox.
I wanted to make those two general points at this time. Certainly the vocational and technical program has proven the need, and the medicare bill which was passed by this house a few months ago showed that the government will take responsibility in some areas. In other areas the government prefers to hide. The only people who will be the losers are the students and the young people of the country who pass through the educational process and move into the mainstream. In these days of easier travel people are not so hesitant to move from one province to another across the land. I am given to understand that one out of every three persons in the United States moves from one part of the United States to another during the course of his lifetime, and similar figures exist for Canada indicating a tremendous movement of people. Yet in respect of those who have the greatest potential for movement throughout the country, namely, our students who receive university education, no federal guide lines or direction are provided.
What is even worse, Mr. Chairman, or could be worse, is the fact that the federal government has refused to impose any conditions upon the moneys provided to the provinces. The provincial grants committees and the university heads are somewhat concerned how the money provided by this transfer of corporation and personal income taxes will be funnelled into the provinces. Let me take, for example, the province of British Columbia where you have the University of British Columbia, a strong and historic institution, competing for funds with Victoria College in Victoria and Simon Fraser University on Burnaby mountain. I have had some association with British Columbia in that I lived there for six or seven years, and I know
March 3, 1967	COMMONS
there are some areas of discontent amongst those three universities, just to pick one province out of the hat. In areas where the federal government withdraws from the educational field I suggest the problems may be compounded. In general, I think it is a retrograde step to ignore the reasoning that was followed when the medicare legislation was passed.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Would the hon. member permit a question?
I was about to conclude. Yes.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Is the hon. member not aware that there is no contradiction in government policy toward education and medicare, because after a five-year study and implementation period we shall turn the administration of the program over to the provinces. It is the same with education. There is a federal-provincial agreement under which we shall turn the program back to the provinces. Exactly the same philosophy applies.

At least with the medicare program guide lines were set out. There were four basic guide lines for provinces wishing to qualify under the medicare program. There are no federal government guide lines in this resolution. The government gave direction under the medicare program; whether one agreed with the principle or not, direction was given; no direction is being given with respect to education.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to make a few brief observations. I must say that on this important and complex resolution that I am not quite as pessimistic as the hon. member who has just resumed his seat about what we shall ultimately obtain with this type of agreement.
I listened to both ministers last night with interest, and listened to the outline of the six principles that are the result of agreements with the provinces. We wholeheartedly endorse these principles as being in keeping with the philosophy of the beginnings of cooperation between the federal and provincial government to meet certain needs and requirements in this country.
Before going further I want to say this: Frequently I run into people who do not seem to realize that no government can give anybody anything, whether that government be federal, provincial or municipal, without taking something away from somebody else. I have met so many people who think that the
Equalization Payments to Provinces government can take something from some other source. They think you can take something out without replacing it. We must show our people in Canada that they can have anything they want, provided they are willing to pay for it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: They are all the same taxpayers.

That is right; they are the same taxpayers. I have had letters recently, not from my constituency, because my people are philosophically sound, but from people in eastern Canada, showing that they have no conception of costs and how these things are met. I do think that this resolution does represent a demonstration of an effort between the federal and provincial governments to get together and to come to agreements with respect to division of taxes and the acceptance of certain responsibilities. To that extent I rejoice in this first step toward, shall I say, what will finally be known as federalism or federal-provincial co-operation.
I listened with great interest to some hon. members speaking about technical and vocational training features of this resolution. I have always been interested in this question. I know there are quite a number of boys and girls dropping out of high school who are not interested in academic training, but who are interested in using their hands and heads in other fields. There is great opportunity here for the development of technical and vocational training and I give the government credit for what has been envisaged to this extent. I hope this program will be continued and improved. There is a great place in Canada for it under present circumstances.
This debate has been informative and interesting. I have risen particularly as a result of the remarks made by the previous speaker. I think members of the house and of the public should be better informed about what happens in federal-provincial conferences on questions of the type we are discussing. Would the minister tell us how this conference was called, or how the arrangements were made for the calling of the conference. What was the general procedure at the conference? Did the provinces one after the other make submissions on topics or did they make a submission in total, with other submissions being made afterwards? How were amendments moved? How was agreement reached between the various provinces during the discussion? What was the general atmosphere, the spirit at these conferences? That is

I think hon. members would like to be informed about how the conference was developed and how it was handled; also, what was the response of the provincial premiers at the conference to the various steps discussed, and to the final agreement that I understand was signed by all provinces? Mr. Chairman, I might answer the last question first by reference to a report of the federal-provincial tax structure committee which met in Ottawa on September 14 and 15, 1966. For those members of the committee interested in knowing the positions of the respective governments, this is the official source of reference. I have tabled all these documents in the house from time to time.
In this document there is an account of the formation of the tax structure committee, the meetings it has held and their outcome. The report I have in my hand is a report of the federal-provincial tax structure committee, and it contains submissions made by the federal government and by each of the provincial governments. When we met subsequently, in October, I, on behalf of the federal government presented further refinements of the federal position based on discussions we had had in September. I made a report to the federal-provincial conference presided over by the Prime Minister. At that conference the Prime Minister confirmed that the proposals put forward by the federal government were in fact the proposals he would recommend to parliament.
The short answer to the other question is that there are no agreements at federal-provincial conferences. Indeed, since there are no written documents as to the division of tax fields or as to the acceptance of equalization payments, and so on, the only agreements reached are for administrative matters such as tax collection agreements. The federal government agrees to collect taxes on behalf of the provincial governments, and to turn revenues over to them.
I can assure the hon. member that when it comes to the division of tax fields the federal government ultimately has to say, "These are [Mr. Herridge.l
DEBATES	March 3, 1967
the taxes we propose to levy" and the provincial governments have to decide that there are other taxes that they propose to levy; and, we hope by consultation and mutual consideration of each other's plans, that we have put together a pattern that is not illogical. I do not think it would be agreeable to this house, for example, if it were to be bound in its decisions of what are appropriate tax policies for Canada through the federal government's entering into agreements with the provinces with respect to the division of tax fields to the point where the freedom of this parliament to legislate with respect to taxes was in any way hampered.
In the bill, to be founded on this resolution, the federal government will be putting forth proposals that it put before the provinces. I can assure the hon. member that not one of the provinces liked them; not one. In fact, in this house we all know that that is not so.
It is true that our prospects for obtaining revenues are better than the prospects of provinces or municipalities, but we have no surplus to turn over. The best we can hope for is that we have taxation systems that are mutually compatible and that permit the economic growth of this country. We shall continue to meet in the future, as provinces meeting with the federal government, to discuss tax problems.

That it is expedient to introduce a measure to provide lor the training of adults wishing to undertake occupational training; to authorize the entering into of contracts with provinces and employers to provide for the payment of the costs incurred in providing occupational training to those adults and to authorize the payment of charges for tuition or otherwise for the training of adults in occupational training courses not operated by a province or an employer; to authorize the payment of training allowances to certain adults undertaking occupational training; to authorize agreements with the provinces respecting research in respect of occupational training and the making of loans to provinces to assist in the purchase or construction of occupational training facilities; to authorize transitional agreements and arrangements with the provinces related to the Technical and Vocational Training Assistance Act; and to provide further for other related and incidental matters.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT OF COSTS, AGREEMENTS WITH PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, last June this house passed the Training Allowances Act. It provided substantially increased training allowances for unemployed workers. In addition, under this act, the workers preserved their unemployment insurance rights while they took training.
As a result of this legislation, the concept of training in Canada has been altered. For the first time, people with adult responsibilities are being granted allowances generous enough to enable them to take training courses. This put an end to the previous dependence of training on the unemployment insurance plan. From here on vocational training ranks with work; it is no longer associated with unemployment or welfare.
The measure I propose today is the logical development of the policy that I had the honour to introduce last year. It is a greatly
Occupational Training
extended program for the training and retraining of members of the labour force. It is an explicit recognition of the federal responsibility for the over-all performance of the economy, and the advancement of the workers on whom that performance depends.
This new program is an integral part of a national manpower policy whose basic purpose is to bring economic opportunity within the reach of Canadian workers.
The resolution proposes to extend training services and training allowances to all persons with adult responsibilities who can benefit from training. Whether a man or woman is eligible for training will not depend on whether he or she is employed, unemployed, underemployed, or self-employed.
The program will respond directly to the person's need for training, not to his statistical classification. The question is whether he will benefit substantially from training, whether it will make his earning power greater in future, whether his contribution to the economy will be increased.
Adult training, as the Economic Council of Canada and many others have pointed out, is one of Canada's most urgent needs. It is a national problem requiring a solution that can be implemented right across the country. But the program must, of course, be administered in full co-operation with the provinces. It must be sensitive to local needs. The federal functions under the program will be discharged by our strengthened and decentralized Canada Manpower Centres. It will be part of the range of services which these centres offer workers who need a second chance to acquire the skills and knowledge they must have to compete in today's dynamic labour market.
I would like to emphasize that this program is not concerned with young people at school but with people who have been in the labour force for some time and intend to stay in it.
This does not mean that the federal government feels that the education of youth is unimportant. Obviously, it is vital to our development. But we are a federal country-which means, though it is often forgotten, that some things that are vital are the responsibility not of this parliament but of the provinces.
The education of youth is a provincial, not a federal responsibility. During the past six years the federal government has contributed greatly to the capital costs of provincial

March 3, 1967
Occupational Training
facilities for technical training. The arrangement was made for six years. It was mostly capital, not operating assistance, because such federal activity in a provincial field could not and should not be thought of as permanent.
Accordingly, the Prime Minister announced last October the termination or phase-out of cost-sharing agreements in this field. Financially, they are more than replaced by unconditional fiscal transfers designed to make it possible for provinces to respond to the rapidly expanding needs of post-secondary education.
Those needs, financially, are very great. But when we think of people, we must recognize that the needs of adults are very different from those of continuing students.
First, there is a financial difference. The adult has been earning an income. He has been using that income to support himself or members of his family. They and he cannot afford to have his income cut off. If he is going to take training, he must be provided with an alternative income from public sources.
The need is in this respect much the same as the need for unemployment insurance. But I think we would all agree that the amount should be appreciably larger. Training is work. And training should not prejudice a man's future protection in the form of his rights to unemployment insurance benefits. What is the same is the principle of an income support.
Second, adult training is different from school education because quite a lot of it can best be carried on, not in a teaching institution, but within industry. This, plainly, is a growing trend. It makes a great deal of sense. But we cannot expect a company to do a great deal of training that may help a man get a job with other firms, unless government bears a good part of the cost.
Third, adult training is most directly related to full employment and improved productivity. It is true, of course, that the quality of education also has an important influence, as young people enter the labour force. The training provided to adults has a direct impact on employment and productivity. Therefore, it is of current, direct concern to the federal government.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)

Obviously, Mr. Chairman, I do not mean that the federal government should provide the training. Provincial governments and in-
[Mr. Marchand.l
dustry are both already in that business and there is no reason for us to join them. But we do have the responsibility for seeing that provincial governments and industry have customers, and that means we have to pay the customers' bills.
This is the responsibility we propose to assume. Instead of being involved 50 per cent and 75 per cent in a variety of technical and vocational education programs, we propose to take 100 per cent financial responsibility for the adult, the person who has left school to earn his living but now needs retraining or further training.
We want to provide a second chance to the people who need it most. These are the men and women who missed the chance to acquire a skill during their youth or whose skill has been made obsolete by technological change. They are the people whose whole lives can be changed, dramatically in many cases, by giving them the occupational training they need.
Occupational training will be provided in courses of 12 months or less. The experience of the last six years has shown what can be accomplished in this way. But it has also shown that many mature adults lack the basic arithmetic, scientific and linguistic facility they need to learn a new occupation. The provinces have developed accelerated courses to provide adults with this background material, and the program will pay for any such basic training that is needed for an occupational skill. To put it another way, our concern is with the skills, but when people must have basic background to learn the skills the program will meet both necessary parts of the total cost.
The provinces have built up extensive systems for providing the type of training adults need. We wish to make use of these facilities and we will pay the provinces for training the adults we refer to their courses.
Occasionally we will need to make use of private training facilities, but we will do so only when a province cannot, at the time, provide the type of training a man needs at a school near where he lives. We will not use private facilities unless it is necessary and the province agrees that it cannot meet the need.
The program will give the employment counsellors in our Canada manpower centres an effective means of helping adult workers adapt to changing occupational and employment conditions. One of the major functions of these centres is to seek out opportunities and make sure that people are aware of
March 3, 1967

them. To discharge this responsibility we must know which occupations to train people for. Misplaced or misguided training is an economic waste and a human tragedy. This is another reason why this program must be implemented through the Canada manpower centres, if it is to be effective and equitable. They will have the necessary information on labour market trends and prospects. This is the only way to keep adult training and retraining closely related to the changing needs of the labour market, and so most helpful to individual workers and employers.
In industry I should make it plain that the program is not designed to pay for the kind of on-the-job training, in a particular job, that is a normal and necessary part of industrial costs. We are concerned with the kind of general training that a worker can take with him from job to job. Where a company provides that kind of training the program will pay both the cost of running the course and an element of reimbursement of the wages the company pays workers while they are learning. But, while the program will normally apply to what might be called "classroom" training in industry, it will also be available for on-the-job training when workers' jobs are threatened by technological change, and extensive retraining by their employer is necessary to help people adapt to new ways of working.
Besides paying living allowances and buying the necessary training services, the program will help provinces to acquire the buildings and equipment to provide the services. This will be done by lending them money to build adult training facilities.
They could take up to 30 years to repay, out of the money the federal government provides, by including the renting of facilities in the costs of the courses we pay for. In effect adult training facilities will cost the provincial taxpayers nothing, and the provinces will have free buildings after 30 years.
The training allowances which will be extended to all trainees who are established members of the labour force will initially be paid at the levels which have been agreed with the provinces under the Training Allowances Act. This means that training allowances will range from $35 to $90 a week as is the case now, depending on family circumstances and living costs. The upper and lower limits will escalate with increases in the general wage level. The actual scales, between those limits, will be settled in consultation with each province so as to fit in with wage conditions in different areas.
Occupational Training
I think, Mr. Chairman, I have made it clear that this program is designed to provide a sounder basis for co-operation with the provinces in the years ahead. That co-operation is essential to the success of all our efforts. It is with the provinces that we will contract for the training services that they and their municipalities provide. When it is necessary to purchase services from private training organizations, that will not be done without provincial agreement. Some provinces already have extensive programs for training in industry; our contributions will be put within the framework that already exists. In addition, we stand ready to share with the provinces the costs of research and development which are needed to establish sound and effective occupational training courses for adults.
The new program outlined in this resolution involves important changes. It moves us from shared-cost agreements with the provinces to different principles of co-operation which I believe will be healthier in every way and give us better value for money. But such a change cannot be implemented abruptly.
On April 1, when the present agreements expire, there will be many people in the midst of courses. To avoid disruption we will continue to share the provincial costs of training such people until they have finished their present courses.
The very substantial capital grants which have been made to the provinces under the current shared-cost arrangements for building secondary, post-secondary and adult and technical and vocational training facilities will be phased out gradually. They will continue at 75 per cent cost-sharing rate until each province has received $480 for every person in its 1961 youth population. In addition, a further $320 per person will be available for the same purpose at a 50 per cent sharing rate. The provinces have already received nearly $600 million through these grants; they will receive a further $550 million under this phase-out arrangement. Funds will be available for exactly the same purposes as before, but there will now be no time limit on their use. In short, this arrangement assures equal treatment for all provinces despite the very different rates at which they have in the past been able to utilize the cost sharing program.
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
Mr. Chairman, I think this is all I need say about this new program at this time. I believe

March 3, 1967
Occupational Training
it is most important. It is a measure which will help the men and women of the Canadian labour force make the adaptations to changing conditions which the world today requires. By making it genuinely possible for people to break out of occupations which offer only under-employment, intermittent unemployment, and poor prospects, we open up new opportunities for people and accelerate the growth and development of our country. We cannot afford any other course of action.
