speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I find it strange that such an incident should occur a second time. Following the comments made by the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Marchand), a member of the party sitting on the Speaker's left asked questions, thus trying to get around the very obvious difficulty of stating his party's position, not knowing what the hon. minister was going to say.
Naturally, since we had no idea of what the minister was going to say, our comments at this stage will be very brief.
In general, I feel that we cannot but commend the proposal being introduced this afternoon, particularly when one considers that it is based on the following principle: a person who is in difficulty, who is unemployed, should not rank among the needy, the beggars, his personal dignity having suffered enough already because of his present unemployment. One must necessarily give favourable consideration to any piece of legislation that will contribute to the development of the human person.
TMr. Marchand.]
Everyone agrees that it is urgent to give reorientation or training to thousands of workers. Everyone is happy to see that new skilled workers are trained and that people are given the means to develop the skills needed because of technological changes and the moving or concentration of industries. Finally, no one can object if the provinces are kept informed of every initiative, if they are called upon to participate and to accept the services offered.
However, some safeguards should be included in the bill when it is introduced. Various efforts were made in the past with regard to retraining and vocational training but they have not necessarily given the results hoped for. That is why it is necessary to go about it with great caution in view of what happened in the past.
For instance, I have in mind the danger that may arise from training formulas concentrating only on the training of skilled labour and on the development of new techniques, because, unless we make sure in advance-and those things happen-that there is a market for such crafts, we will find ourselves in a situation where, instead of having one unemployed tinsmith in a given area, we will have, if there are eight applicants, nine unemployed tinsmiths. There will always be a very close relationship to be established between the crafts to be developed and the market open to those who are going to engage in such crafts, considering particularly that you have to ascertain not only the crafts and occupations required, but also to what extent people willing to train will agree to move to where opportunities are, once they have received that training.
Mention has been made recently of mines in outlying areas in urgent need of skilled workers. Let us suppose that people were trained in a central place to meet that requirement. If those people refuse to go where jobs are available, they will have been trained to no avail and it will be necessary to start all over again and offer them another type of training. Therefore, it will be most interesting to study the provisions of the bill to be submitted.
There is, I am sure, some contradiction in the fact that professional training opportunities are being provided when, at the same time, the number of existing training centres is being reduced. I am referring particularly to the phasing out of the vocational schools where it would possibly be more practical to ensure that such premises are fully utilized.
March 3, 1967



This afternoon, during discussion on the preceding resolution, occasional mention was made of education and provincial rights. I think it must be fully realized that any province demanding its provincial rights is not seeking autonomy as an end in itself, but as a means to ensure the development of its heritage and of its citizens.
In such a case, any new situation likely to affect the well-being and the normal development of the citizens should always have a certain priority. This justifies, for instance, the direction and the measures which the federal government wants to present to the provinces, even though they might accept or reject them. The fact that the provinces are sensitive about some fields which, up to now, were considered for specific reasons areas of provincial responsibility, must not restrict the initiatives that the federal government must take, with regard to the full development of our national economy. I am sure that the provinces need no particular spokesman, in one corner of the house or another, to state their rights. The provinces have all the necessary means to put a stop to it if, at one time or another, they feel that there is a negative encroachment on their rights.
Something special may come out of this initiative in the field of training. We talk more and more about training through television, for instance.
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
I believe that education through television is possible in this field. If provincial authorities denied residents the opportunity to take part in training programs through the television medium, claiming exclusive rights in the field of education and training, these authorities would have a very difficult time trying to explain these restrictions imposed on the citizen.
We speak of training. speechtext:
I am sure the broad general principles enunciated by the minister will be welcomed by every member of the house and by every person who has looked at the problem in respect of full employment, and manpower training and retraining in our complex society. Having said that we greet the general principles warmly I must say that if one compares what the minister said today with the results of past programs he will realize the tremendous distance we must cover in the next year or two to implement the things about which the minister spoke.
We welcome the announcement of the minister that training allowances will be paid by the government to people taking training, and that this will in no way jeopardize unemployment insurance benefits. We also welcomed the announcement that 100 per cent of the bills for retraining of students will be paid by the government. This is precisely what I suggested during an earlier debate in relation to tax arrangements, namely that the federal government should accept its responsibilities to help those people who come from or live in have-not provinces.
We will be watching very carefully the details as to how the minister proposes to do these things. We will carefully scrutinize the estimates of the minister's department, the number of centres that will be open and the number of people who are trained. There is, however, a tremendous if not immeasurable gulf between these broad general principles enunciated by the minister and the realities of situations.
Mr. George Bain has an article in the Globe and Mail today under the heading "Have Job-Will Travel". Mr. Bain does have a job and does travel. This article was written in Stockholm and deals with a program which has been in existence in Sweden for a number of years. I commend this article to the minister because it outlines a program which works, and which is far superior to anything this or any other government has established to date. This is the kind of program which if emulated, would allow this government to accomplish a great deal.
Mr. Bain points out that in Sweden the national labour market board, which does essentially the job carried out by the minister's department in Canada, is empowered to retrain a Swedish worker, to pay his and his wife's way to another town to look after a

March 3, 1967
Occupational Training
new job, to help him while he gets settled there, to support her and the family in the old place until he can find a home for them, and to move them. This board can even buy the old house, if it happens to be in a part of the country where the population is declining and the person being moved could sell it otherwise only at a loss.
Mr. Bain spells out some of the details of this program. In part he writes:
An unemployed, or about-to-beeome-unemployed worker, can obtain retraining which may extend up to two years. His basic monthly allowance during that period will be $90 (allowing five Swedish crowns to the dollar), plus $15 lor his wife, and $12 a month for each child-$129 in all, for a man with two children.
(If the same man has to leave his home area to take retraining, he will get about 1,100 Swedish crowns a month, or $220, the amount being flexible to include the total cost of his rent. In all cases, these allowances are tax free.)
Later on Mr. Bain writes this:
For instance, to help provide for the upkeep of his family while he finds a new home for them, the worker who goes to a new place is entitled for 12 months to $44 a month for his wife, $12 for each child, moving expenses when they move, and a so-called installation grant of $411, plus $30 for each child, to help get the new home going.
This is the kind of program which has been in existence for some time in Sweden. It seems to be the kind of program the minister was referring to in broad generalities, but it is not the kind of program we have had in Canada up to now. We have had training programs, but I suppose one could not expect that a training program which started late should be successful at the beginning.
People who have been close to workers and unemployed people, such as representatives of trade unions, whether or not they are affiliated with the Canadian Labour Congress or the Confederation of National Trade Unions, have known from firsthand observation that these training programs were not working.
Program No. 5 had from its inception a fantastically high drop-out rate because the allowances were inadequate. The individuals taking advantage of that program could not continue to do so because they could not maintain their families. It was obvious to these workers and everybody else that if they finished the program they would get better work at higher rates of pay, but that was little consolation when they could not afford to keep their families.
It is true that we have increased very substantially the amounts allowed. However, I think we have to keep a constant eye on
[Mr. Orlikow.l
whether we are doing enough so that workers who are unemployed will be persuaded that it pays them and their families to make the effort to study under the retraining programs which will be offered, so that they can improve themselves.
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
One of the difficulties we have had in the past, and which we continue to have in a country as large as Canada, is that very often the jobs available-and in the period of high economic activity which we are now experiencing there is a great number of jobs available-in Hamilton, Toronto or Vancouver, to mention just three of the areas in which there is the highest rate of economic activity, are of little use to the unemployed worker in Newfoundland, Cape Breton or the Gaspe peninsula, even if he has the training to fill the job which is open, if he cannot afford to move his family. When we study the details of the program which the government will be instituting, and when we study in particular the question of retraining, we will have to consider this fact because there will be little purpose in retraining people if we do not enable them to move to the kind of jobs which they have been trained to fill.
The fact is that we have not had this kind of training program in the past. Mr. J. Fenwick, assistant to the director of the largest district covered by the United Steelworkers of America has given particular attention to this problem. In a speech made to a conference convened by the Canadian Labour Congress to deal with manpower training, held about this time last year, he reported that a survey of almost 100,000 workers carried out by their union showed that the training program on the job covered only 1,400 workers out of that group. This is just not good enough. In the same survey it was found that the basic steel fabricating, aluminum and mining companies had only 505 apprentices. Again this is not good enough. While I commend the government for the program establishing these manpower training centres which the minister has announced, it is my opinion that, even though the federal government is prepared to put up substantially more money than it has done in the past, the program will fail unless the people involved are made aware of it, unless they are told the kind of allowances that will be paid and the kind of training which they can receive.
Until now this information has not been made available so that one union leader after
March 3, 1967

another has reported that his members and the workers with whom he has come in contact are almost completely ignorant of the existing training programs. I hope the new Department of Manpower and Immigration will set up advisory committees of labour and industry so that the information about the kind of programs which the minister has announced today will be made available to unions and to management, and that the minister and his department will go out, in cooperation with labour and management, and do a selling job to convince people that there is hope for them, that they should avail themselves of the opportunities which are now being provided by the government, and that it is in their interest and in the interest of their families that they avail themselves of the retraining programs and thus upgrade their skills and knowledge.
We may have heard an excellent speech from the minister, and he may have enunciated very important principles which will be useful to the working population of Canada, but without this kind of aggressive program of education and salesmanship-although I am not particularly enthused by the term "salesmanship"-I am afraid that this program will fail, as have past programs.
In closing I would urge the minister, in introducing the bill, to give the members of the house the information requested by my colleague, the hon. member for York South, as to the amount of money which the government envisages will be allocated to this program over the next two or three years, the number of people it is expected can be trained, the number of manpower centres which will be established, and all the other information which was requested, so that the house can be assured that the government is serious about this program, that it intends to proceed with the retraining of the people of Canada who need the kind of training about which the minister has spoken, and so that we can get a meaningful program rather than just the excellent speeches we have so often heard in the last half dozen years.

speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-38, to amend the Criminal Code (provincial lotteries).

He said: Mr. Speaker, for the fifth consecutive year I have the honour to introduce a bill to amend section 179 of the Criminal Code, in order to make an exception to that legislation and enable or authorize provincial governments, which would like to do so, to establish their own provincial schemes intended solely and strictly for provincial purposes, especially welfare and education as well as any other responsibility falling under the exclusive jurisdiction of the provinces.
Mr. Speaker, I have made five attempts to try to convince my colleagues of the House of Commons by substantive arguments, reports of investigations and finally by indications of popular opinion, that it is time for the government to change its policy on this matter and yield to the evidence that a majority of people is asking that provincial governments be authorized to legalize the organization of lotteries in provinces.
During previous discussions, certain members representing various parties in the house have supported the substance and the letter of the legislation which I introduced during those past years.
All the spokesmen of the parties have approved the principle that I would like to stress, and no one has opposed either this bill or its implications.
Unfortunately, however, they resorted to the well-known process of stifling with praise and kind words this bill which I shall again attempt to have accepted by this house. I hope that today the house will express its views by a vote, and that we shall not have recourse to dilatory practices to prevent the passage of a bill which seems to fulfil the wishes of the public at large.
I wish to thank the N.D.P. and Social Credit members, and even the government members who supported me in the past in my efforts initiated many years ago while I tried to persuade my colleagues that it was high time for the house to take a clear and definite stand on this matter.
Since I failed in my attempts, Mr. Speaker, I decided to conduct a national investigation
March 3, 1967

myself, that is, I attempted to ascertain the consensus of opinion in each province. It seems to me that the work I performed was incumbent upon the governmental authorities, particularly the Minister of Justice and Attorney General (Mr. Cardin) who is responsible for such an amendment. Well, owing to the department's inertia, I would say, in this respect, I personally undertook to conduct such an investigation.
I am happy to have the opportunity today to let my colleagues in the house know the results of this investigation conducted through most of the Canadian municipalities, either through the mayor himself or through the municipal councils.
Over the past two years I have sent a questionnaire to many Canadian municipalities from Halifax to Vancouver, including the Northwest Territories. I wanted to establish unequivocally whether Canadians in general, and provincial residents in particular would favour an amendment to the Criminal Code in order to allow the provinces to have their own lottery system.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
Mr. Speaker, I have here a large collection of these questionnaires that I had sent to the mayors. I urge hon. members to consult this huge file. Every answer has been listed, province by province, in that record which I am ready to put at the disposal of the Department of Justice so that it can confirm or invalidate the result of that investigation which leaves no doubt concerning the general approval of my initiatives and those of a great number of Canadians who devoted themselves in the past to advocate this idea of provincial lotteries.
I wish to emphasize the splendid work done over many years by one Mrs. English, of Calgary, who gathered more than 500,000 signatures for a petition in favour of the establishment of a lottery in Canada, a few years ago.
The result of my investigation supports that petition and, moreover, adds opinions from each of the provinces.
For instance, from the province of Manitoba, where 1 sent 43 questionnaires, I received 18 answers, 11 of which were for and 7 against. From Saskatchewan, out of the 44 questionnaires I forwarded, I received 23 answers, 20 favourable and 3 unfavourable. In Alberta, 31 municipalities answered favourably and 6 unfavourably. Out of the 86 questionnaires sent to British Columbia, I received 56 answers, 47 of which were favourable
Criminal Code Amendment and only 4 unfavourable. In the Northwest Territories, I sent one questionnaire and the answer was unfavourable. From Newfoundland, out of 21 municipalities, 7 answered favourably and one unfavourably. From Prince Edward Island, two declared themselves in favour and none against. From Nova Scotia, out of 19 answers received, 13 were favourable and 2 unfavourable. From New Brunswick, out of 14 answers, 8 were favourable and 3 unfavourable. Ontario, of course, gave much more significant answers, in view of the great number of municipalities in that province. Out of the 233 questionnaires I sent, I received 111 answers, 94 of which were favourable and 8 only were opposed. In the province of Quebec, out of the 207 questionnaires I sent, I received 135 answers, 134 were favourable and one opposed.
Mr. Speaker, out of 428 replies received from municipalities across the land, 367 were in favour of provincial lotteries and only 36 were against. That is a clear and explicit expression of the Canadian people's opinion on the possibility of setting up a system of provincially operated lotteries.
Now, in the light of such obvious and favourable replies, I wonder why the Minister of Justice (Mr. Cardin) and the government still hesitate, even today, to vote on this bill, so that hon. members might have a chance of expressing their views. If hon. members truly wish to express an opinion which reflects the wishes and desires of the people they represent here, there is no doubt that the house will amend the Criminal Code so as to authorize the provinces to set up their own system of lotteries.
That is the problem in many circles which fear some small groups of reactionaries, of bigots and I would even say of chauvinists who, out of personal conviction or taking their stand on a principle supposedly connected with public morality, object to the government amending the Criminal Code and allowing the establishment of provincial lotteries.
Now, Mr. Speaker, with all due respect for the views of such people, I feel that if it is to be argued that lotteries are against public morality, those people should be told that there are some criteria making it possible to determine whether or not lotteries are against public morality. Mr. Speaker, there are three such criteria.
If the lottery is free from fraud and under government control for the common good, I believe that, in such a case, public morals are
13746	COMMONS
Criminal Code Amendment not involved and the argument of the opposing groups does not stand.
On the other hand, it more than statistics or inquiries are required to prove the desirability of establishing a lottery, I suggest that the house refer to the views expressed by the provincial premiers themselves.
During the federal-provincial conference held in Ottawa in November 1963, the question of a provincial lottery was brought up. At that time, some provincial premiers as well as the Prime Minister of Canada expressed their views.
On being questioned at the end of one of these conferences, Mr. Robichaud, premier of New Brunswick, stated that his province had no firm idea on this problem, although he was not opposed to a lottery.
Mr. Lesage, then premier of Quebec province, is supposed to have said: If lotteries were legalized, they could provide additional revenues to the province, which greatly needs them.
On the other hand, Mr. Robarts, premier of Ontario, expressed a favourable opinion by stating that he was for the minor amendments to legalize bingos and other ancillary lotteries.
Prince Edward Island, British Columbia, and Alberta are opposed in principle, but they are not against the expression of opinions. They did not bring forward any denial and they did not make any formal opposition.
The present Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) also expressed a personal opinion at the conclusion of this conference, and I quote his words:
The establishment of a federal lottery does not interest the central government, but amendment to criminal code will be examined in the light of the views expressed by the provinces.
Now, you see, Mr. Speaker, these are extremely serious thoughts, allowing the members or permitting them, if they so desire, to express their views and vote on this question, since we are aware of the opinions of several prime ministers, federal or provincial, and we have at our disposal the results of some popular surveys which leave no doubt on the increasing popularity of the idea.
Some time ago, I took part in some radio and television broadcasts on this matter, and I am happy to tell my colleagues that I have received over 1,200 letters from viewers and listeners who encouraged my efforts to convince the government that the time has come to act and to have the house decide on this question.

DEBATES	March 3, 1967
There are also many social groups which have endorsed the legalization of lotteries, and still do, at the federal as well as the provincial level, as I am suggesting.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
On November 19, 1963, there has been the Quebec Federation of School Boards. In its report, the Royal Commission on Health Services in Canada had advanced this possibility.
In a brief submitted to the Royal Commission on April 17, 1962, "L'Association des medecins de langue frangaise du Canada, Quebec section, had also endorsed this idea. The United Textile Workers of America had also supported this view during a congress held in Trois-Rivieres.
The Canadian federation of mayors and municipalities had also approved this opinion on jVIay 31, 1963. On December 19, 1962, the Quebec Boards of trade had also agreed on the possibility of amending the Criminal Code in favour of lotteries.
The Canadian Railway Workers Federation, in a brief submitted to the federal government, also endorsed lotteries. And many organizations have supported and expressed opinions in favour of legislation to permit the setting up of provincial lotteries.
Now, Mr. Speaker, several advantages could be outlined in favour of lotteries. I will simply summarize five major ones to my way of thinking.
First, this legislation would leave the provinces entirely free to act or not to act in this field.
Second, the setting up of Canadian lotteries would stop the drain of our money to foreign countries; as reported in certain quarters, this amounts to something like $150 to $200 million per year.
It would also put a check on the illegal lotteries which are found in such great numbers in all the big cities of Canada. A provincial lottery would also be a source of employment for people who for lack of qualifications can only hold part-time jobs or do general work.
Fifth, it would be for the provinces a source of income voluntarily fed by the people and which could be used for provincial purposes exclusively.
There are throughout the world over 70 countries which operate a lottery and recently in the United States the state of New York, following the state of New Jersey, decided to operate its own lottery. What we are waiting
March 3, 1967	COMMONS
for in Canada is to do the same and assume our responsibilities.
Mr. Speaker, after five years of work and discussions, after a number of bills introduced exactly in that same spirit by colleagues in this house, the time has come to vote on that matter.
I note that some of my Social Credit colleagues have also put a bill similar to mine on the order paper. If in the past five years there have been discussions and investigations, and if even federal-provincial conferences have put this item on their agenda, so as to allow discussions on the advisability of amending the Criminal Code in order to legalize lotteries in the provinces, I wonder why we, legislators, are waiting to settle this matter.
Those who for reasons of political partisanship will object or practise obstruction, as is too often done in this house, in order to kill such a bill, will be answerable to their constituents whom they represent in the Commons. They will be answerable to public opinion in their riding.
A few years ago-I can see the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Pepin) bursting out laughing. He does not seem to fear the opinion of his constituents. Perhaps he is callous and has joined, in his complacency, the former Quebec premier who paid for it through defeat during the last provincial election. But if hon. members of this house, especially those who represent Quebec ridings, do not realize that 80 per cent of the people of that province have declared themselves in favour of a provincial lottery and if the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Pepin) is so energetic, why does he persist in objecting to a bill which answers and meets the aspirations of 80 per cent of the people who are called upon to elect him?
If for reasons of partisanship, some hon. members refuse to voice their opinions by a vote, they will have to account for it to those who are responsible for their election.
A few years ago a colleague of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, the hon. member for Saint-Maurice-Lafleche (Mr. Chretien) presented Bill No. C-2, to change the name of Trans-Canada Air Lines into Air Canada and, during the hour set aside for consideration of public bills, opposition members co-operated with the hon. member.
At that time, the bill to change Trans-Canada Air Lines' name into Air Canada was 23033-869
Criminal Code Amendment adopted, because we showed political responsibility in this house.
I urge members on the government side and the minister to call for a vote. That is not complicated and I know that by voting, we will be acting responsibly towards our constituents whom we represent in this house.

subtopic: MEASURE TO PERMIT PROVINCIAL GOVERNMENTS TO CONDUCT LOTTERIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, three private members bills relating to lotteries have been introduced during the present session of parliament, Bill No. C-38 being introduced by the hon. member for Sainte-Marie (Mr. Valade) who has just resumed his seat, Bill No. C-42 by the hon. member for Sherbrooke (Mr. Allard) and Bill No. C-84 by the hon. member for Essex West (Mr. Gray). The first two bills would amend section 179 of the Criminal Code, to permit a lottery organized and operated by a provincial government, where the purpose is, in the one case "to provide financial assistance to hospitals or for other welfare purposes, under provincial jurisdiction" or in the other case to provide "for payment in the province of additional amounts with respect to family allowances and old age pensions".
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
Bill C-84 sponsored by the hon. member for Essex West would repeal the provisions of section 168 which deals with common gaming houses, and would give certain immunities to social clubs, charitable and religious organizations, and would further repeal section 179 dealing with lotteries to give certain immunities to charitable and religious bazaars and allow a wider exemption for games and lotteries held by private charitable organizations, provided the gain to the organization is expended for a charitable purpose within six months. It would seem that recent stories about the financial success of lotteries in such places as New Hampshire in the United States, New South Wales in Australia, and New Zealand, have stimulated interest in this subject.
Bill C-42 immediately follows Bill C-38 on the public bills list, and it may be that today's debate will be continued in private members hour a week hence, as the subject matter of both bills is practically the same. There would seem to be little likelihood of Bill C-84 being reached in the present session, as it is No. 42 on the order paper.
Mr. Speaker, the last official inquiry in Canada into the policy of lotteries, including bingo and similar games, was made by a joint
13748	COMMONS
Criminal Code Amendment committee of the Senate and House of Commons which made its report on July 31, 1956. The report recommended several minor clarifications of the lottery provisions of the Criminal Code and some comparatively minor relaxations in favour of charitable purposes, but it recommended expressly against state lotteries. It was recommended that three types of lotteries be permitted as follows:
1.	Lotteries licensed under provincial authority in aid of charitable, religious and community purposes, provided the retail value of prizes offered by any one organization does not exceed $5,000 in any year, promotion expenses are prohibited, expenses such as rent and advertising are restricted, and audited reports are submitted to the licensing authority.
2.	Small raffles of goods, without licence, in connection with non-commercial gatherings, provided the raffle is merely incidental to the gathering and the prizes do not exceed $50 in total value.
3.	All midways at agricultural fairs, as presently allowed, with the further concession that agricultural fair associations be permitted, if licensed, to hold lotteries for prizes not exceeding a total of $10,000 yearly in connection with the presale of admission tickets.
The question of lotteries, particularly state lotteries, was discussed at the federal-provincial conference held in November, 1963 and the attitude of the provinces differed widely. Quebec put the case for state lotteries. Nova Scotia was not interested in a state lottery, but favoured some relaxation in favour of small raffles. Alberta, British Columbia and Saskatchewan were opposed to state lotteries. Manitoba expressed interest in the legalizing of off-track betting. Prince Edward Island expressed some interest in the New Hampshire scheme. Newfoundland did not take up a position. New Brunswick was not interested, itself, in conducting a state lottery, but had no objection to an amendment which would permit another province to do so. Ontario took somewhat the same position as New Brunswick, although it anticipated enforcement problems should a state lottery be set up in a neighbouring province. All these attitudes were informally stated. At the conclusion of the 1963 conference, the following press release was issued:
Some provincial governments explained the difficulties they have in enforcing the provisions of the Criminal Code in respect of lotteries and gambling. Suggestions were made that the institution of provincial lotteries would alleviate this situation. Other provinces, however, opposed this suggestion. The federal government indicated that

DEBATES	March 3, 1967
it had no interest in instituting a federal lottery but undertook to consider the amendment of the Criminal Code in the light of the view put forward.
The matter was considered again at the conference of attorneys-general on organized crime held in Ottawa on January 6, and 7, 1966. At this conference, provincial attitudes again varied widely and may be summarized as follows: Quebec again put the case for state lotteries under provincial auspices, expressing the view that such lotteries would help eliminate rackets in this field. Manitoba favoured some relaxation of the present provisions in favour of charitable and benevolent organizations, under provincial licence, the conditions to be uniform and stated in the Criminal Code; by implication it was against state lotteries. British Columbia was completely opposed to state lotteries; it considered that racketeers manage to get into even charitable and benevolent lotteries and that it is impossible to carve out a government niche free from danger of such intrusions.
Spokesmen for the province challenged the Quebec view that state lotteries would solve the racket problem and considered a review of the gambling laws to be more important than that of the lotteries laws, because gambling is one of the most important areas of organized criminal activity in Canada. They suggested an all party committee of the House of Commons to study gambling laws. Saskatchewan referred with approbation to a working paper which has been discussed by the criminal law section of the conference on uniformity of legislation in 1960; by implication Saskatchewan appeared to be against state lotteries. This working paper comprised a draft revision of the lottery sections designed to implement substantially the recommendations of the 1956 joint committee. The views of the section were in line with those of the joint committee, to the effect that any relaxation of the law should be in the field of charities. Ontario had no instructions upon, and no interest in, state lotteries, but it was not opposed to small charitable lotteries governed by the Criminal Code.

Nova Scotia was against state lotteries in Nova Scotia and in any other province because a state lottery in another province would put Nova Scotia in a very difficult political position. At the conclusion of the conference of January, 1966, the following statement was issued:
The government of Canada will consider lotteries and the gaming sections along with all other amendments to the Criminal Code suggested at this conference. As to lotteries and the gaming sections the report of the Senate and House of Commons committee, other representations received, the views expressed at this conference and the work already done in the Department of Justice will be examined and considered in the department and a report made to the government.
The reply that the Department of Justice has been making to all persons who have written to make representations, for or against state lotteries, or relaxation of the gaming and lottery provisions in their application to charitable organizations, is to refer to the statements issued following the federal-provincial conference of November, 1963, and that of January, 1966, and to state that the opinions received upon this somewhat controversial subject will be carefully considered in connection with the review that is now under way.
Generally speaking, Mr. Speaker, most of the churches have expressed themselves as opposed to state lotteries and to any extension of the immunities given to charitable and religious organizations, the Church of England going so far as to ask to be expressly excluded from such immunities.
Strong representations in favour of relaxing the immunities in favour of charitable organizations have come from certain service clubs. Representations in favour of state sweepstakes have come from various organizations and individuals, and particularly the Quebec government.
It is interesting to consider the experience of the United Kingdom where small pools and lotteries are legal. There have been two royal commissions on lotteries and betting in the United Kingdom since 1930. The first one sat in 1932 and 1933, and the second one in parts of the years 1949 and 1951. The 1932-33 report recommended against the institution of large lotteries in the United Kingdom, but said that if it should be decided to permit the institution of any large lottery, the least objectionable form would be a state lottery for the benefit of the exchequer. Of course we have to bear in mind here that the United Kingdom is a unitary state, whereas we are a 23033-8691
Criminal Code Amendment federation of federal government and ten provinces.
The 1949-51 commission considered the question of national lotteries as part of an inquiry into the whole field of gambling. Generally speaking, it did not find that gambling in moderation had any serious, economic, social or moral consequences. It did not believe, however, that the state should take a direct part in providing gambling facilities unless there were special reasons therefor. Approaching the question of a national lottery from these viewpoints, it said it did not consider that a lottery is a form of gambling which is likely to lead to excessive expenditure on the part of individuals or to an undue preoccupation with gambling.
It expressed the view that the estimate of revenue which may be obtained from a national lottery is usually greatly exaggerated by the supporters of the proposal, and it thought that a national lottery would add to rather than displace existing forms of gambling.
The commission said it did not overlook certain advantages of a national lottery: It was cheap to run; made no great demands on manpower; avoided any undesirable forms of advertising and inducement; assured honesty in administration; could be regulated in size to correspond with current economic conditions, and could be abolished without affecting vested interests. The commission concluded, however, that there was no important advantage to be gained by establishing a national lottery and no reason, therefore, to depart from the general principle that it is undesirable for the state to make itself responsible for the provision of gambling facilities.

Mr. Speaker, as one who favours public control and public operation of lotteries I wish to say a few brief words. I do not intend to talk out this measure because I support the hon. member's proposal. First, it seems to me we should keep in mind that the question today is not whether we want to have lotteries: We have them. The last estimate I received showed we have 28 separate illegal lotteries operating in Canada.
Gambling and drinking are two of the world's most ancient frailties, and for a long time past governments have acted to control drinking. At present some 30 countries in the world have acted to control forms of gambling. In this country we have control of gambling at the race tracks, and some people would also say we have had control of gambling in the stock markets for many years.

DEBATES	March 3, 1967
I think we should have governmental control, provincial or federal, of publicly operated lotteries. One of the facts in support of this proposal is that at the present time many millions of dollars are leaving our country every year to go to privately and publicly operated lotteries in other countries, and it seems to me logical that we should try to keep this money at home.
A very modest estimate of sweepstake or lottery revenue for a province the size of my own, British Columbia, with quarterly lotteries conducted by the government, is that it would amount to over $1 million a year in extra public revenue. I look on the idea of a lottery conducted by a provincial or a federal government as an indirect or do-it-yourself tax. I believe that nowadays, when we are looking for revenue, we should not overlook any additional way to obtain it. Canada is one of the dwindling number of countries which do not have some form of government operated lottery. Over 30 different countries now have lotteries.

Finally, I would urge support of the hon. member's bill from the point of view of a respect for law. At present we have so many illegal sweepstakes and lotteries which are operated in Canada that the law is in great disrespect. If we cannot bring this to a vote tonight, I should like to see this bill and one or two others like it referred to a committee such as the committee on justice and legal affairs. This committee could consider these bills jointly as has been done in respect of other proposals, and recommendations could be made. I should like to see this come to a vote.

On the other hand, I disagree with the bill as it is introduced by the hon. member because it is much too summary and we cannot see our way clear. First, in order that some lotteries may be instituted, of course, we need a government bill and not a private bill.
Second, in this private bill-this is its essential weakness-the operational structure of the lotteries is not outlined. How are we to rely on a bill so short and so simple to determine the existence of lotteries in the province and in the country?
Third, there is need for a uniform legislation in the country. Now, the bill leaves it up to the provinces to establish their own lottery, without knowing exactly what will happen in the other provinces. The province of Quebec may have lotteries, but supposing that Ontario and Manitoba prohibit lotteries, what might happen, if not a confusion which it will be difficult to prevent.
In view of such pitiable deficiencies, we are not in a position, for the time being, to say that the hon. member's bill should be passed. However, we can say-at least I can say so on my own behalf-that we will support the principle of such a legislation.
